bigPicture: Tension in the Gulf continued: the US said it shot down two Iranian drones heading for Bahrain and denied Iran's claim to have destroyed a US radar there, as Israel's spy chief held talks in Washington. US wholesale inflation hit 6.5% a year, the highest since 2022, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield to about 5.16% and strengthening bets on a December Fed rate rise; chip stocks fell sharply again after Nvidia's CEO quit. In Europe, the Kremlin set conditions for European participation in Ukraine talks and EU leaders refused to put their own security on the table. Taiwan said China had massed more than 100 ships in drills, the IEA said the oil market is turning to surplus, and a Microsoft outage disrupted governments and businesses worldwide for a second day.

stories.everyday: Each flare-up around the Gulf adds a 'risk premium' to oil, which flows into petrol, diesel and heating prices, including in Poland. Higher energy costs also feed inflation and can keep interest rates, and so loan payments, higher.
stories.rankWhy: A live US–Iran confrontation next to the Strait of Hormuz keeps the world's most important oil route, and fuel prices everywhere, at risk.

sources.name: Middle East Monitor: CENTCOM denies Iranian claim, says 2 drones shot down
Al Jazeera: US denies Iran's claim it hit radar in Bahrain
VINnews: Mossad chief visits Washington as Netanyahu presses Trump

stories.title: US shoots down two Iranian drones aimed at Bahrain and denies Iran hit its radar; Israel's spy chief is in Washington as Netanyahu presses for renewed strikes
stories.what: US Central Command (CENTCOM, the US military command for the Middle East) said on Friday that US forces shot down two Iranian one-way attack drones launched toward Bahrain, with no injuries or damage, and called false the claim by Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) that it had destroyed a US early-warning radar there, Middle East Monitor and Khaleej Times reported. The IRGC said its strike answered an attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, a port in southern Iran; Al Jazeera said it was the first claimed Iranian attack on US military assets in a Gulf country since early September. Mossad director Roman Gofman was in Washington for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, according to three sources cited in reports, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presses President Trump to resume combat against Iran; Trump has so far preferred a naval blockade and economic pressure. Separately, Turkey and Qatar signed a defence pact on Friday, Khaleej Times reported.
stories.why: Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy's 5th Fleet, so attacks there test whether the pause in large-scale US strikes holds. Trump has said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states preferred a waiting period, while Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in Israel's 27 October election, wants military action, VINnews reported, citing sources; some Israeli opposition figures fear he could try to provoke an attack before a new government forms. Every sign of escalation raises the risk to tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, which is why oil traders watch each incident.

stories.everyday: A higher US yield and a stronger dollar matter in Poland: the dollar was close to 4 zł on Friday, which makes dollar-priced fuel and goods dearer. Higher global rates can also keep Polish bond yields, and so some loan costs, elevated.
stories.rankWhy: US inflation at the factory gate is running at a four-year high, pushing the world's benchmark borrowing cost above 5% and cementing bets on a Fed rate rise that would tighten money worldwide.

stories.title: US wholesale inflation hits 6.5%, the highest since 2022; the 10-year Treasury yield climbs to about 5.16% as markets bet on a December Fed hike
stories.what: US producer prices (the PPI, which tracks prices businesses receive for goods and services) rose 0.3% in October, slightly less than the 0.4% economists expected, but were up 6.5% from a year earlier, the biggest annual rise since November 2022, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics data reported by Stock Titan. September's monthly rise was revised up to 1.4%; 'core' PPI excluding food and energy rose 0.3% in October and 5.0% over 12 months. The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to about 5.16% on Friday, its highest since October, from about 5.10% on Thursday, as traders priced in a possible December rate rise, Yahoo Finance and TradingNews reported. The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75%–4% on 28 October, with two officials voting for a hike.
stories.why: Wholesale prices often pass through to consumer prices with a lag, so a 6.5% annual rise suggests inflation pressure is still building after this year's oil shock. If the Fed raises rates on 9 December, borrowing becomes dearer across the US economy; higher US yields also attract money into dollars, which weighs on other currencies and on gold, which pays no interest. German market reports (Ariva/dpa-AFX) said markets now treat a December hike as nearly certain.

stories.everyday: Big tech and chip companies are a large share of global index funds, so their falls show up in many pension and savings plans, including Polish PPK and IKE funds that hold world equities.
stories.rankWhy: A sharp sell-off in chipmakers, the stocks that drove the AI boom, hits the biggest companies in global indices and pension portfolios.

stories.title: Chip stocks slump again: AMD falls about 10% and the Nasdaq drops nearly 2% by midday; US senators ask Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify
stories.what: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX, a basket of US-listed chipmakers) was down 4.2% shortly after Friday's open, TokenPost reported. Around 11:00 New York time AMD was down about 9.7%, Broadcom about 6.8%, Applied Materials 6.2% despite a record quarter, and Nvidia 4.7% at $158.43, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 1.85% and the S&P 500 1.1%, TradingNews reported; the Dow was roughly flat. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify over 'national security concerns' about chip exports, with hearings requested in early December, Fortune reported (it gave 3 December for Huang; the committee's post named 10 December for Lutnick). Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy; Trump said the FBI is investigating.
stories.why: Investors are weighing whether Nvidia's leadership crisis and the political fallout could bring tighter export controls on AI chips to China, which would hurt sales across the industry, strefainwestorow.pl noted. At the same time, rising bond yields make future profits worth less today, which hits richly valued tech shares hardest. Nvidia reports results on Tuesday 17 November, its first under interim CEO Colette Kress.

stories.everyday: For people in Poland the outcome decides how secure the eastern flank feels, how much the state spends on defence, and whether energy and trade with the east ever normalise.
stories.rankWhy: Who sits at the table, and whether Russia's demands reach beyond Ukraine to NATO members, shapes the security of the whole of Europe, Poland included.

sources.name: Reuters via ThePrint: Russia says Europeans can join talks if they show readiness
Reuters via ThePrint: Europe's security cannot be part of peace talks, EU leaders say

stories.title: Kremlin says Europe must first show 'readiness to contribute' before joining Ukraine talks; Merz calls it 'the same old game' as a report lists sweeping Russian demands
stories.what: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow would decide on European participation in Ukraine peace talks only once Europe showed a 'genuine intention and readiness to contribute', a day after US negotiators said President Vladimir Putin had agreed to include Europeans, Reuters reported. In Dublin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called this 'the same old game' and said there would be no talks about Europe without Europe; EU leaders said Europe's security set-up should not be part of the negotiations, and Latvia's prime minister called such talks 'a trap'. Germany's Bild reported informal Russian proposals that would give Russia all of Donbas, bar NATO bases in the Baltic states and return Finland to its pre-NATO status; Peskov said Finland's NATO exit 'was not discussed'. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said it was not up to Russia to decide who represents the EU.
stories.why: Russia wants a broad new European security order negotiated before the details of the war, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this week, while European governments fear that would trade away their own security. Poland, the Baltic and Nordic states warned on Thursday against such brainstorming, a European diplomat told Reuters. The talks so far, in Abu Dhabi and Moscow, have shown some progress but no breakthrough on territory, both sides said.

stories.everyday: Most of the world's advanced chips are made in Taiwan, so any threat to its sea lanes could affect the price and availability of phones, cars and computers, including in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: A naval show of force around Taiwan, the island that makes most of the world's advanced chips, raises the risk premium on a region at the heart of global supply chains.

sources.name: Reuters via Star-Advertiser: China stages unannounced Pacific drills
Kyiv Post: China simulates attacks on Taiwan before Xi–Trump talks

stories.title: China massed more than 100 ships in unannounced Pacific drills, Taiwan says, calling it 'silent intimidation' before next week's APEC summit
stories.what: China's military and coast guard had more than 100 vessels in the western Pacific and around Taiwan at one point in early November, and about 70 were still operating inside the 'first island chain' on Friday, Taiwanese security officials told Reuters. The officials said the drills, larger than the 'Justice Mission 2025' exercise held nearly a year ago, included simulated attacks on Taiwan and other militaries and involved three theatre commands and the Liaoning carrier group. China says the carrier is on routine exercises not aimed at any country; its defence ministry did not respond to Reuters. Beijing hosts the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on 18–19 November, where Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet.
stories.why: Taiwan officials said coordinating fleets from three commands looks like rehearsal for a blockade, while keeping the drills unnamed avoids a diplomatic backlash, a foreign intelligence source said. Xi gave a speech on Thursday urging peaceful reunification without mentioning force. The timing, just before high-level meetings, signals pressure on Taipei and Washington.

stories.everyday: If the surplus holds, pump prices in Europe should ease over time, though the IEA notes diesel in Europe remains expensive. Poland's capped prices for this weekend are 6.02 zł for Pb95 and 7.52 zł for diesel, strefainwestorow.pl reported.
stories.rankWhy: The world's energy watchdog says the oil shortage caused by the Iran war is turning into a surplus, which matters for fuel prices and inflation everywhere.

HDFC Sky: Brent slips as oil heads for second weekly decline
AP via News4Jax: Asian shares mixed

stories.title: IEA says the oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover; Brent hovers around $95–96
stories.what: The International Energy Agency (IEA), which advises mainly rich oil-importing countries, said in its monthly report that world oil supply will average 105 million barrels a day (bpd) in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd above demand, after previously forecasting a deficit, Reuters reported. It expects 2026 demand to fall by 2.7 million bpd to 102.3 million bpd because high prices have curbed use, and a surplus of about 3.8 million bpd in 2027. Middle East exports are recovering faster than demand despite tanker attacks, it said. Brent traded around $95.5–96.2 a barrel during Friday, up from about $72 in late February before the Iran war, according to HDFC Sky, TradingNews and AP.
stories.why: A surplus means more oil is produced than used, so stocks build up and prices tend to fall, unless supply is disrupted again. That is why prices hardly moved: traders balance the IEA's numbers against fresh risks around Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi facilities. US crude stocks also rose 4.7 million barrels in the week to 6 November, against expectations of a fall, the US EIA reported.

stories.everyday: When work email and video calls stop, offices, hospitals and public services slow down; Polish firms and institutions that rely on Microsoft 365 were among those affected, strefainwestorow.pl said, citing bank and government services.
stories.rankWhy: An outage of Microsoft's email and workplace tools for more than a day disrupted governments, police, courts and businesses in dozens of countries.

sources.name: Al Jazeera: Microsoft hit by global outages, what happened and why

stories.title: Microsoft's global outage of Outlook, Teams and Copilot drags into a second day; the company says it was not a cyberattack
stories.what: Users began reporting they could not reach Outlook at about 16:00 GMT on Thursday, and the disruption was still unresolved on Friday, with Downdetector logging at least 43,000 Outlook reports from 72 countries at about 07:00 GMT, Al Jazeera reported. Teams and Copilot were also disrupted, and affected users included government systems in Singapore and Japan, the Philippine Supreme Court and Australia's federal police. Microsoft said there was no indication of malicious activity, that some servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, and that it was rolling back a network change while having only 'marginal success' restoring services; later on Friday it reported continued recovery progress, CBS News and Euronews reported. Microsoft shares fell before the open but were roughly flat by midday in New York, according to market reports.
stories.why: Much of the world's office work now runs on a few cloud providers, so a failure in one company's servers spreads instantly across countries and sectors. Microsoft has not published a root cause, so it is not yet clear why fixes initially failed.

stories.everyday: The nuclear dispute is one of the main reasons the Gulf war could flare again, which would hit oil and gas prices that Polish households pay for.
stories.rankWhy: Without inspections nobody can verify Iran's near-weapons-grade uranium, which feeds the risk of renewed war in the Gulf.

sources.name: AP via ClickOrlando: Iran tells UN nuclear agency monitoring cannot proceed
Al Jazeera: UN watchdog calls on Iran to reopen nuclear facilities

stories.title: UN nuclear watchdog says it cannot verify Iran's near-weapons-grade uranium and is 'increasingly concerned' about an uninspected enrichment plant
stories.what: A confidential report by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), circulated to member states on Friday and seen by AP, called the lack of information on Iran's nuclear sites and material a 'matter of proliferation concern' needing urgent correction. The IAEA said it does not know the exact location of an underground enrichment plant near Isfahan that Iran declared in June 2025, or whether it holds nuclear material; it has not been able to verify Iran's stock of 440.9 kg of uranium enriched up to 60%. Iran told the agency that talks on resuming monitoring cannot proceed while it faces military threats from the US president, AP and Al Jazeera reported. Since June 2025 the only site inspected has been the Bushehr power plant.
stories.why: Uranium enriched to 60% is a short technical step from the roughly 90% used in weapons, so not knowing where it is fuels arguments for and against new strikes. Iran says it remains committed to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and blames US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation, while the IAEA says it is ready to return at short notice.

stories.everyday: Polish factories sell much of their output to Germany and France, so slower growth there can mean fewer orders and slower wage growth here, even though Poland itself is growing faster.
stories.rankWhy: Slower growth in the euro area, Poland's biggest export market, with France shrinking, affects jobs and orders across Europe.

sources.name: Eunews: EU GDP up 0.5% in Q3

stories.title: Euro-area growth slows to 0.4% in the third quarter as France's economy shrinks; the bloc swings to a trade deficit on energy imports
stories.what: The euro area's economy grew 0.4% in July–September compared with the previous quarter, down from 0.6%, and the wider EU grew 0.5%, Eurostat estimated; year on year, growth was 1.3% and 1.5%. France contracted by 0.1%, Germany grew 0.2%, Italy was flat, Spain grew 0.6% and Poland 0.8%, Eunews reported. In September the euro area ran a goods trade deficit of €10.3 billion, against a €13.5 billion surplus a year earlier, as the energy import bill rose to €37.6 billion.
stories.why: Higher energy prices since the Iran war mean Europe pays more for imports, which drains money out of the economy and turns trade surpluses into deficits. Weak growth in France and Germany limits demand for goods from suppliers such as Poland. The International Monetary Fund's Europe director Mateusz Szczurek said the structure of Europe's economy needs to change faster, Euronews reported.

stories.everyday: Poland is a major supplier of parts to German car factories, so cuts in Germany can reach Polish plants and jobs over time.
stories.rankWhy: A freeze on investment by one of Germany's flagship carmakers signals deeper trouble for an industry that employs hundreds of thousands, including Polish suppliers.

sources.name: RTÉ (Reuters): Mercedes-Benz to halt German investments
Euronews: Mercedes-Benz halts new investment in German plants

stories.title: Mercedes-Benz halts all new investment in its German plants and explores closures after failing to agree labour-cost cuts
stories.what: Mercedes-Benz has halted further investment in its German locations and is exploring closing sites because of high manufacturing costs in Germany, according to a company memo seen by Reuters and reported by RTÉ. Production chief Michael Schiebe said management could not agree labour-cost reductions with the works council and unions; board member Britta Seeger said the company wants to avoid closures but must now examine that option. Talks with the IG Metall union are continuing. Consultancy Roland Berger warns at least 200,000 car-industry jobs could be lost in Germany by 2030.
stories.why: German carmakers face high energy and labour costs and fierce competition from Chinese brands, while China itself has stopped being a big profit driver, RTÉ reported. Volkswagen is preparing its biggest-ever restructuring and Schaeffler is cutting jobs, so Mercedes' move adds to pressure on the whole sector.

stories.everyday: Attacks on refineries and power grids affect energy markets and keep the risk of incidents near Poland's border high.
stories.rankWhy: The war's daily toll continues on both sides even as diplomacy intensifies, affecting civilians and energy infrastructure.

Africanews: Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv hospital

stories.title: Russia says it downed 1,198 Ukrainian drones overnight; Russian drones set a Kyiv hospital on fire and kill two in Odesa
stories.what: Russia's defence ministry said its air defences destroyed 1,198 Ukrainian drones over more than 15 regions overnight, and four people were killed in an industrial zone in the Volgograd region that includes an oil refinery, RTÉ reported. In Kyiv a Russian drone started a fire that partly destroyed the second floor of a medical facility; 30 people were evacuated and seven rescued, Africanews reported. In Odesa two people were killed and five injured, and a 17-year-old boy was killed in Zaporizhzhia, RTÉ said.
stories.why: Both sides are trying to strengthen their position while negotiators discuss a settlement; Ukraine targets Russian refineries to cut fuel revenue, while Russia's strikes hit Ukrainian cities and energy. Neither side's claims can be independently verified.

stories.everyday: For internet users in Poland, the veto means no new national fast-track for removing illegal posts or appealing platform decisions for now; EU-level rules still apply to the largest platforms.
stories.rankWhy: The veto leaves Poland, reportedly the last EU state not fully applying the EU's online-content law, without a fast way to remove illegal material, and risks EU penalties.

sources.name: Wirtualnemedia: President vetoes law on blocking illegal content

stories.title: President Nawrocki vetoes a law to speed up removal of illegal online content; the government says it was meant to protect children
stories.what: President Karol Nawrocki vetoed an amendment that would have implemented the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA, the EU law on how online platforms must handle illegal content), Wirtualnemedia and Polsat News reported. The bill would have created a fast procedure for the Digital Services Coordinator to order removal or blocking of illegal material, required child sexual abuse material to be removed within 24 hours, and let users challenge platforms' moderation decisions. Nawrocki argued that courts, not officials, should decide what is illegal and warned of a 'censor official'; Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the president bears personal responsibility, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the veto blocks protection of children. On the same day the president signed laws on land for the CPK airport project, anti-terror rules and pharmacy advertising, strefainwestorow.pl reported.
stories.why: The dispute is about balance: faster removal of hate speech and abuse versus the risk of officials blocking lawful speech. Poland is reported to be the last EU member not fully applying the DSA, which could lead to proceedings and fines at the EU Court of Justice, Wirtualnemedia said; it did not confirm such proceedings have started.

stories.everyday: Ebola has also been reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria; the risk to Europe is considered low, but weak outbreak control anywhere increases the chance of spread.
stories.rankWhy: The world's second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record is being fought by unpaid, under-supplied workers while hundreds of millions of dollars are unaccounted for.

sources.name: Daily News Egypt Africa: MSF says Congo responders unpaid
allAfrica: All of Africa Today, 13 Nov
UN News: Unrest fuelled by armed groups holds back response

stories.title: MSF says Ebola money is not reaching Congo's frontline workers; Africa CDC says $700 million of disbursed funds is unaccounted for
stories.what: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a report six months into the response that Ebola responders in the Democratic Republic of Congo are unpaid, poorly trained and short of supplies, with some ambulances out of fuel, Daily News Egypt and allAfrica reported. About 11,000 people have been infected and more than 5,400 have died since the outbreak was declared in May; the BBC has described it as the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. Africa CDC said $700 million of the $962 million disbursed to implementing organisations is unaccounted for; its chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to call it embezzlement. Two-thirds of deaths happen in communities rather than treatment centres, MSF said.
stories.why: The Bundibugyo strain behind this outbreak has no approved vaccine or treatment, so control depends on tracing contacts and isolating patients, which needs paid, equipped staff. Armed groups in eastern Congo also hinder the response, the UN said. Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said only 22% of aid agencies had provided the details needed for oversight.

stories.everyday: Without shelter, the UK ambassador warned, people face hypothermia, respiratory infections and waterborne disease; the crisis also shapes EU diplomacy and public debate in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: About 1.7 million Gazans live in tents or damaged buildings as winter arrives, and 53 states say aid is still below agreed levels.

sources.name: The National: 53 countries urge Israel to open Gaza to unrestricted aid

stories.title: 53 countries urge Israel's incoming government to open Gaza to unrestricted aid as winter floods threaten 1.7 million people in shelters
stories.what: A joint statement led by Britain, Qatar and Jordan and backed by 53 UN member states and other organisations urged Israel's incoming government to let aid into Gaza through all crossings and to protect health and aid workers, The National reported. It said aid is still below levels required by UN Security Council Resolution 2803. UNICEF estimates about 1.7 million of Gaza's 2.2 million people live in tents, makeshift shelters or damaged buildings, almost one million in flood-risk areas. On Thursday an Israeli strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis killed 10 people; Israel said it targeted a senior Hamas commander, which Hamas denied.
stories.why: A 2025 ceasefire has largely reduced fighting, but Israel continues regular strikes and controls what enters Gaza; more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, according to Gaza's health ministry. UN aid chief Tom Fletcher said waiting for a new Israeli government is not an acceptable excuse for delays in winter supplies.

stories.everyday: Anyone using video calls for work can be targeted: be suspicious of requests to run scripts or paste commands to 'fix audio', even from a familiar face.
stories.rankWhy: A North Korean scam using stolen webcam videos took over $400 million and hit hundreds of targets in 58 countries, showing how deepfake-style fraud now works at scale.

sources.name: Nextgov/FCW: FBI disrupts North Korean fake-call scheme

stories.title: FBI disrupts North Korean 'FaceStealer' scheme that used fake video calls to steal over $400 million in crypto
stories.what: The FBI disrupted a North Korean hacking campaign, dubbed FaceStealer, that officials said netted more than $400 million in stolen cryptocurrency, Nextgov reported. Hackers secretly recorded victims' webcams, then used that footage in fake Zoom or Teams meetings to impersonate them to their contacts and trick others into installing malware. Authorities seized cloud servers and more than 900 victim videos; security firm Arctic Wolf said more than 677 targets in 58 countries were identified. Separately, the Justice Department got court authorisation to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion stolen from the exchange Binance last month, a theft the FBI attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.
stories.why: Crypto theft is a major source of hard currency for North Korea under sanctions, and video-call impersonation exploits the trust people place in seeing a familiar face. A senior official said recovering funds is getting harder because hackers split them into small amounts across laundering networks.

stories.everyday: Climate deals shape EU rules that Poland must follow, such as emission costs on coal power and heating, which feed into electricity and heating bills.
stories.rankWhy: Whether nearly 200 countries agree any path away from oil, gas and coal shapes climate risks and energy investment for decades.

sources.name: Reuters via Al-Monitor: UN chief urges drastic emissions cuts as COP31 wrestles with fossil fuels

stories.title: COP31 in Antalya struggles over fossil fuels as UN chief Guterres urges 'immediate and drastic' emission cuts
stories.what: UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an immediate and drastic reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and urged big emitters to keep the 1.5°C goal alive, Reuters reported via Al-Monitor. Major fossil-fuel producers and consumers are resisting firm new targets: Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally opposed limits, India and the G77 group of developing countries reportedly oppose fuel-specific language, while Brazil backs national roadmaps away from fossil fuels. Host Turkey wants a global electrification plan at the centre of a deal; the EU supports it if the electricity is clean. Australia, the lead negotiator, will take submissions until Saturday and plans a draft political text early next week; the US is skipping the talks for a second year.
stories.why: A UN report found the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C of warming, so pressure is high, but countries that depend on fossil-fuel income or cheap coal fear for their growth. COP decisions need consensus, which favours vague wording.

stories.everyday: A weak yen makes Japanese cars, electronics and holidays in Japan cheaper for foreigners, including Poles, but adds to global currency volatility.
stories.rankWhy: A yen near 160 per dollar raises import costs for Japan and keeps the threat of intervention hanging over currency markets.

sources.name: investingLive: Katayama warns of one-sided yen moves

stories.title: Yen hovers near 160 per dollar; Japan's finance minister warns of 'one-sided, rapid' moves and says she will coordinate with the US Treasury
stories.what: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said she sees one-sided and rapid moves in currency markets and will communicate with the US Treasury to respond appropriately, but declined to comment on intervention, investingLive reported. The dollar traded around 159.9–160 yen on Friday (AP). The government is also bringing forward winter utility-bill subsidies. In July the US Treasury bought yen, its first such intervention since 1998, after the yen reached a similar level.
stories.why: US interest rates are far higher than Japan's, so investors earn more holding dollars, which pushes the yen down; bets on a Fed hike widen that gap further. A weak yen makes imported energy and food dearer for Japanese households.

stories.everyday: Crypto prices swing far more than shares; a 10% monthly fall shows the risk for anyone holding them.
stories.rankWhy: Bitcoin's slide below $70,000 shows how higher interest rates drain money from the riskiest assets.

sources.name: Yahoo Finance live: stock market today, 13 Nov

stories.title: Bitcoin drops below $70,000 for the first time in nearly three months as rate-hike bets and fund outflows weigh
stories.what: Bitcoin fell below $70,000 early on Friday for the first time in nearly three months, dipping to about $68,000 before recovering to around $69,265, and is down more than 10% in November, Yahoo Finance reported. It was about $68,867, down 3.8%, at about 10:00 New York time, TheStreet reported. Analysts cited expectations of further Fed rate rises, continued outflows from spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, the unwinding of leveraged bets, and MSCI's removal of Strategy from two US indices.
stories.why: Bitcoin pays no interest, so when safe US bonds yield above 5%, holding it becomes less attractive; leveraged traders forced to sell can then speed up the fall.

stories.everyday: When Europe's gas supply tightens, wholesale prices rise, which can feed into heating and electricity bills, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The EU still pays billions for Russian LNG weeks before a full ban, which matters for energy security and for Russia's revenues.

sources.name: Urgewald: EU's Russian Arctic LNG bill balloons to €8.7 billion

stories.title: EU paid about €8.7 billion for Russian Arctic LNG in ten months, 50 days before a full import ban, campaign group says
stories.what: The EU paid an estimated €8.7 billion for liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Russia's Yamal project in January–October 2026, about 21% more than in all of 2025, the German group Urgewald estimated from Kpler shipping data. 177 cargoes and 12.89 million tonnes reached EU ports; Belgium was the largest destination over the period and France took 70% of October deliveries. A full EU ban on Russian LNG under existing long-term contracts takes effect on 1 January 2027. Urgewald said the figures are indicative estimates, not verified contract payments.
stories.why: Europe needs gas to refill storage, now below 72% against a five-year average near 89%, and Russian cargoes remained legal under long-term contracts until the ban starts.

stories.everyday: If storage is not built, industries such as cement and steel in Europe, including Poland, may face higher costs for their emissions.
stories.rankWhy: An oil major's legal challenge to an EU climate rule tests whether Europe can make producers pay for carbon storage.

sources.name: Euronews: ExxonMobil sues EU over carbon storage rules

stories.title: ExxonMobil takes legal action against the EU over a rule forcing oil and gas producers to build carbon storage
stories.what: Three ExxonMobil companies filed a notice of arbitration against the EU under the Energy Charter Treaty, challenging the carbon-storage part of the EU's Net Zero Industry Act, Euronews reported. The act sets an EU target of at least 50 million tonnes a year of CO₂ injection capacity by the end of 2030, with oil and gas producers required to contribute. Exxon argues the obligation is impossible to meet because of slow permits and high costs and says the EU breached treaty protections; the European Commission said it does not comment on ongoing cases.
stories.why: Carbon capture and storage (pumping CO₂ underground) is seen by the EU as necessary for heavy industry, but projects are expensive; who pays is a central dispute in climate policy.

stories.everyday: Measles also circulates in Europe; checking that children and adults have had two doses of the MMR vaccine is the main protection.
stories.rankWhy: The worst US measles outbreak in decades is testing whether the country keeps its 'measles-free' status.

sources.name: Reuters via Taylorville Daily News: US measles cases rise to 5,412

stories.title: US measles cases reach 5,412 this year, with six deaths, as experts weigh the country's 'measles-free' status
stories.what: The CDC reported 5,412 measles cases this year as of 12 November, up 230 from its previous update, with 591 hospitalisations and six confirmed deaths, Reuters reported. Case counts above 5,000 are the first since 1991. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,505 cases. A Pan American Health Organization commission is expected to decide soon whether the US keeps its measles-elimination status.
stories.why: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases; outbreaks spread where vaccination rates fall below the roughly 95% needed for community protection.

stories.everyday: The case shows how votes are counted locally and why accurate protocols matter for every voter.
stories.rankWhy: Charges against election officials touch public trust in how Polish votes are counted.

sources.name: Portal Samorządowy (PAP): over 130 commission members charged

stories.title: More than 130 polling-station officials in Poland charged over flawed counting in the 2025 presidential runoff
stories.what: Prosecutors in Siedlce have charged more than 130 members of local electoral commissions with failing to perform their duties by miscounting valid and invalid votes in the second round of the 2025 presidential election and drafting protocols incorrectly, PAP reported via Portal Samorządowy. The offence carries a fine, restriction of liberty or up to two years in prison. Investigators found the errors distorted results for one of the two candidates in the affected commissions; the report did not say the overall outcome changed.
stories.why: Counting at thousands of polling stations relies on volunteers and local officials, so mistakes can occur; prosecuting them is meant to protect confidence in elections.

stories.everyday: If rates stay unchanged, monthly payments on variable-rate loans linked to the reference rate also stay roughly the same for now.
stories.rankWhy: Poland's external balance and rate outlook affect the złoty and loan costs for millions of households.
stories.title: Poland's current-account deficit far smaller than expected in September; MPC member says rates could stay on hold in December
stories.what: Poland's current account showed a deficit of €718 million in September, against a consensus forecast of a €2.58 billion deficit; exports rose 9.7% and imports 11.9% year on year, both below forecasts, strefainwestorow.pl reported, citing central bank data. Monetary Policy Council (RPP) member Janczyk said the council may keep rates unchanged in December, with later decisions depending on regulated energy prices. NBP governor Adam Glapiński said Poland needs cheaper energy, AI adoption and competitive exports to keep growing fast. The złoty was steady at about 4.41 per euro on Friday afternoon (Forsal).
stories.why: A smaller deficit means Poland needs less foreign money to finance its spending abroad, which supports the złoty; the RPP watches energy prices because they drive inflation, which was 3.5% in October.

stories.everyday: The leader of the Senate influences US decisions on budgets, sanctions and support for Ukraine, which matter for Europe.
stories.rankWhy: A contest for the leadership of the incoming Democratic Senate majority will shape how the US Congress deals with the president.

sources.name: PBS NewsHour: Van Hollen to challenge Schumer

stories.title: Senator Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer to lead the Senate Democrats, who won a majority in the midterms
stories.what: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday that he will run for leader of the Senate Democrats in the next Congress, challenging Chuck Schumer and saying the party needs new leadership, PBS NewsHour reported. Democrats won control of the Senate in the midterm elections; Schumer cited '55 seats and counting'. The secret-ballot leadership vote is expected in early December and would be the first contested Senate Democratic leadership election in decades.
stories.why: The Senate majority leader controls which bills and nominations reach a vote, so the choice shapes how Congress uses its new majority.

stories.rankWhy: Brazil's budget repair matters for Latin America's largest economy and its currency.

sources.name: The Rio Times: Latin America pulse, 13 Nov

stories.title: Brazil's Senate approves the core of Lula's fiscal adjustment bill; amendment votes follow on 17 November
stories.what: Brazil's Senate approved the base text of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's fiscal adjustment bill by 45 votes to 31, with four amendment votes scheduled for 17 November before the bill goes to the lower house, The Rio Times reported. The government says it will improve the 2027 budget balance. The real weakened about 1% to around 5.64 per dollar by midday as the dollar strengthened globally.
stories.why: Investors watch whether governments can control deficits; credible fiscal plans can lower borrowing costs, while doubts weaken the currency.

sources.name: Al Jazeera: Indonesia vice president resigns amid eligibility dispute
Jakarta Globe: Gibran offers to resign

stories.title: Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigns over a dispute about his eligibility; parliament has 60 days to pick a successor
stories.what: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the son of former president Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and parliament on Thursday 12 November, and Prabowo accepted it 'with a heavy heart', Al Jazeera reported. The Constitutional Court and Supreme Court ruled last month that documents on his overseas schooling did not meet election requirements. Under the constitution, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) must choose a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days; no new election is held.
stories.why: The rulings undermined his eligibility for the 2024 vice-presidential race, and 120 lawmakers had started a process that could have led to impeachment. The resignation comes amid protests over the economy, corruption and the handling of wildfires, Al Jazeera said.

stories.everyday: Shrinking glaciers and snow cover affect water supplies, farming and flood risk, including in European mountain regions.
stories.rankWhy: A new study in Science says Earth's ice is being pushed beyond safe limits, with long-term effects on sea levels and water supplies.

sources.name: PIK Potsdam: Cryosphere decline beyond safe planetary limits

stories.title: Earth's ice, glaciers and permafrost have been pushed beyond a 'safe operating space', a study in Science finds
stories.what: Human-driven climate change is degrading ice sheets, mountain glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover beyond a proposed 'safe operating space for the cryosphere', according to a study published in Science on 13 November and led by the Stockholm Resilience Centre with researchers from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, the institutes said. The authors warn of growing long-term risks to ecosystems and human societies.
stories.why: Melting ice raises sea levels and changes river flows that billions of people rely on; once ice sheets lose mass, recovery takes centuries.
